---
title: "Worked example — auditing a replication package"
subtitle: "Take a folder of inherited code and turn it into something a stranger could run."
---

The single highest-value use of agentic coding for an empirical economist
is **replication-package work**. Whether you're preparing a package for
submission, refereeing one, or trying to run a coauthor's old project on
a fresh machine, the pattern is the same: someone has to read every file,
trace dependencies, and figure out why the master script breaks on line
237. Claude Code is unusually good at this.

This page walks through both directions: **auditing** a package you've
inherited or are refereeing, and **building** one from your own working
project for journal submission.

## Setup

```bash
cd ~/Dropbox/Projects/wage-paper-replication
claude
```

Same orientation pass as always:

> "Read the project. List every file. For each subfolder, tell me what it
> appears to contain. Identify any 'master' script — something a user
> would run to reproduce the results."

## Direction A — auditing an existing package

### Step 1 — produce a dependency map

> "I want a dependency map of this replication package. Trace which scripts
> read which raw data files, which scripts produce which intermediate
> data files, which intermediate files are inputs to which analysis
> scripts, and which analysis scripts produce which tables/figures in the
> paper. Output as a Markdown list. Don't run anything yet."

This is the kind of task that takes a careful human a full day. Claude
will do it in a few minutes, and it will catch things like "table_3.do
reads `clean_data_v2.dta` but no script in the package produces
`clean_data_v2.dta` — only `clean_data_v3.dta`." That's the bug you're
hunting for.

### Step 2 — identify what's missing

> "Based on the dependency map, list everything required to reproduce this
> paper that is **not** in the package: missing raw data files, missing
> intermediate files that no script produces, packages or libraries used
> in the code but not declared, hard-coded paths that point outside the
> package."

Claude will give you a clean punch list. Common findings:

- A path like `/Users/coauthor/Dropbox/...` hardcoded into a `.do` file.
- A `library(haven)` call without `haven` declared in a `requirements.R`
  or `renv.lock`.
- A `merge` step that requires a file you got from the IRB and didn't put
  in the package.

### Step 3 — try to actually run it

> "Try to run the master script. If you hit an error, stop, tell me what
> happened, and propose a minimal fix. Don't auto-fix anything — just
> propose."

This is the test that matters. A package that "should run" and a package
that *runs on a clean machine* are different things. Claude is patient
about this loop in a way humans are not.

::: {.callout-warning}
For Stata, R, etc., Claude can call out to your installed interpreter.
**Make sure you're running in the right environment** — the same Stata
version your coauthor used, the same R packages, etc. If you're refereeing,
this is part of the audit: the package should declare its environment.
:::

### Step 4 — document the gaps

> "Write a `REVIEW.md` that lists everything I'd ask the authors to fix
> before this package is ready for publication. Group by severity: blockers
> (won't run at all), important (runs but doesn't reproduce a result),
> minor (style/clarity)."

You now have your referee report's "replication" section, drafted in 30
minutes instead of 3 days.

## Direction B — building a package from your own project

You've got a paper accepted; the journal wants a replication package.

### Step 1 — inventory what you actually used

> "Look at every script in this project. List the ones that produce
> something cited in `paper.tex` (a number, a table, a figure). Anything
> not on that list is dead code or exploratory work that doesn't belong
> in the public package."

### Step 2 — produce a clean structure

> "Propose a folder structure for a public replication package: separate
> raw data, intermediate data, code, output. Don't touch the files yet —
> just propose the layout."

Approve the proposal.

> "Now reorganize accordingly, *copying* (not moving) files from the
> current project into a new `replication-package/` directory. Update
> path references in scripts so the package is self-contained."

::: {.callout-warning}
Have Claude **copy, not move**. Replication-package surgery is a one-way
trip if you let it move things; you want your working project untouched
until you're sure the package builds.
:::

### Step 3 — write the README the way the AEA wants it

> "Write a `README.md` for this replication package following the AEA
> data and code availability standards: data sources and access,
> computational requirements (software, packages, expected runtime),
> instructions to run, and a mapping from each table/figure in the paper
> to the script and output file that produces it."

This README is the single most important document in your package. Read it
critically — Claude can write a plausible-looking one that overstates
how complete the package is.

### Step 4 — confirm reproducibility on a fresh state

> "Pretend you've never seen this project before. Following only the
> README, run every step from scratch. Stop and tell me if anything is
> ambiguous, missing, or fails."

This is the test you can't easily run yourself — your machine has all
your packages installed and your data sitting around. Claude can simulate
the cold-start experience.

## Why this is the highest-value use case

- **Tedious.** Every step is mechanical but requires care.
- **Error-prone for humans.** Reading 40 files in order is exactly the
  task we're worst at.
- **High stakes.** A package that doesn't reproduce is a paper that gets
  flagged by the data editor. A package with hardcoded paths is a paper
  that the field can't build on.
- **Easy to verify.** "Does it run on a fresh machine?" is a binary test.
  You'll know if Claude's audit was right.

## Common traps

::: {.callout-warning}
**Claude can hallucinate that a script produces a table.** Always
spot-check the dependency map against a few of the actual results. Open
the script Claude says produces Table 3, check that it does.
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
**Don't let Claude commit changes to your real project automatically.**
Especially during reorganization, you want a manual checkpoint. Use
[plan mode](../getting-started/plan-mode-and-todo.qmd) for the destructive
steps.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
**Build a `/audit-replication` slash command.** If you do this twice, write
a skill — see [Memory, CLAUDE.md, skills](../workflow/memory-and-claude-md.qmd).
Your `myccskills` repo is the right place for it.
:::
